extraction_text: Krishna (also referred to as Shauri, Madhava, Janardana, and Keshava) spoke to the assembled Yadus and then ascended his great chariot, which was equipped with all weapons and yoked to his horses.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Chariot made by Vishvakarma (the divine architect), flagpole topped with Garuda (the eagle mount of Vishnu)

extraction_text: Arjuna and King Yudhishthira (also referred to as Dharmaraja) joined Krishna on the chariot.

attributes.relationships: Krishna is Arjuna's charioteer and close friend; Yudhishthira is the eldest Pandava brother and king.

extraction_text: Krishna drove the chariot swiftly in pursuit of Bhima (also referred to as Vrikodara, son of Kunti).

attributes.relationships: Bhima is the second Pandava brother; they are pursuing him to stop his vengeance.

extraction_text: Bhima, driven by rage and a desire for revenge, could not be stopped by his pursuers and rode to the banks of the Bhagirathi River.
At the river, Bhima saw the sage Vyasa (also referred to as Krishna Dvaipayana, son of Satyavati) sitting with other sages, and nearby he saw Ashvatthama (son of Drona) in an ascetic state.

attributes.relationships: Ashvatthama is the son of Drona, the slain Kuru teacher; he is an enemy of the Pandavas.
attributes.description: Ashvatthama was wearing bark garments, smeared with ghee, covered in dust, with dishevelled hair.

extraction_text: Bhima charged toward Ashvatthama, shouting for him to stand and fight.

attributes.emotional_state: Bhima is aggressive; Ashvatthama is initially fearful

extraction_text: Ashvatthama, seeing Bhima armed and Krishna's chariot approaching with Arjuna and Yudhishthira, panicked but then resolved to use a supreme divine weapon (Brahmastra).

attributes.supernatural_elements: Summoning of the Brahmastra, a celestial weapon
attributes.emotional_state: Ashvatthama's fear turns to desperate resolve

extraction_text: Ashvatthama, in anger, uttered the command 'Kill the sons of Pandu!' and released the weapon, which produced a fire capable of destroying the three worlds.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Weapon creates apocalyptic fire like that of the end of the world (Yama)
attributes.intent: To annihilate the Pandavas and potentially the entire world

extraction_text: Krishna (Vasudeva) recognized Ashvatthaman's intention and advised Arjuna to use the divine weapon taught by Drona.

attributes.relationships: Krishna guides Arjuna; Ashvatthaman is Drona's son and enemy

extraction_text: Arjuna descended from his chariot, blessed Ashvatthaman, himself, and his brothers, then invoked his divine weapon to counter Ashvatthaman's.
Both divine weapons unleashed, creating apocalyptic effects: blazing flames, comets, winds, terror, and shaking earth.
Sages Narada and Vyasa intervened to stop the weapons, standing between them to protect the three worlds.
Arjuna expressed concern that withdrawing his weapon would leave them vulnerable to Ashvatthaman's, but the sages insisted on restraint.
Arjuna successfully withdrew his divine weapon, a feat only possible for someone of perfect soul and celibate vows.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Divine weapon control requiring spiritual purity

extraction_text: Ashwatthama (Drona's son) cannot recall the Brahmastra weapon he unleashed.

attributes.reason: He did not observe celibacy (Brahmacharya) and unleashed it with anger and intent to kill

extraction_text: Ashwatthama explains his situation to Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana).

attributes.details: He unleashed the weapon out of fear of Bhima, to save his own life, and with anger and intent to kill the Pandavas (sons of Pritha/Kunti)

extraction_text: Vyasa explains Arjuna's actions and virtues.

attributes.details: Arjuna (also called Vijaya) observed celibacy, kept his vows, respected elders, and mastered the Brahmastra. He unleashed his Brahmastra not out of anger or to kill Ashwatthama, but to counter Ashwatthama's weapon, and then recalled it successfully.

extraction_text: Vyasa warns of consequences if the Brahmastra weapons destroy each other.

attributes.supernatural_element: If the Brahmastra weapons destroy each other, the kingdom will suffer a 12-year drought.
attributes.reason_given: Arjuna refrains from destroying Ashwatthama's weapon to protect all beings.

extraction_text: Vyasa advises Ashwatthama to recall his weapon and offer his jewel (Mani) to the Pandavas.

attributes.proposal: Ashwatthama should recall his weapon, calm his anger, and give his powerful protective jewel to the Pandavas in exchange for his life. Yudhishthira (eldest Pandava) does not wish to win through unlawful means.

extraction_text: Ashwatthama agrees to give up his jewel but states his unleashed weapon cannot be made futile.

attributes.details: He agrees to give the jewel due to Vyasa's words but declares the unleashed weapon (the reed arrow) will not be in vain; it will fall into the wombs of the Pandava women.
attributes.supernatural_element: The weapon is redirected to target the Pandava lineage.

extraction_text: Vyasa instructs Ashwatthama to use his weapon on the wombs of the Pandava women and then stop.
Ashwatthama, in great pain, hurls his celestial weapon into the wombs of the Pandava women.

Krishna confirms Ashwatthama's evil act and tells him a prophecy: a Brahmin saw Uttarā (daughter of Virata and wife of Abhimanyu) and said her son would be born after the Kuru extermination and would be the reviver of the lineage.

attributes.relationship: Krishna confronts Ashwatthama about his crime

extraction_text: Ashwatthama angrily replies that his weapon will kill Uttarā's fetus, despite Krishna's protection.
Krishna curses Ashwatthama: the fetus will die but be revived and live long; Ashwatthama will wander the earth for 3000 years, diseased, alone, and shunned.
Krishna describes Parikshit (the revived child) as virtuous, skilled in weapons, and ruling for 60 years, demonstrating his own ascetic power.

attributes.relationship: Parikshit will restore the Kuru lineage

extraction_text: Vyasa condemns Ashwatthama's cruelty and affirms Krishna's curse will come true.
Ashwatthama accepts his fate, gives his jewel to the Pandava brothers, and departs for the forest as they watch.
The Pandava brothers honor Krishna, Vyasa, and Narada.
The Pandavas and Krishna return to their camp with the celestial gem (mani) taken from Ashvatthaman.
They find Draupadi in deep sorrow, fasting due to the death of her sons.
Bhima, following King Yudhishthira's command, gives Draupadi the celestial gem and recounts their vengeance.

attributes.details: Bhima tells Draupadi that Duryodhana has been killed, he drank Duhshasana's blood, and Ashvatthaman was defeated but spared as he is a Brahmin's son

extraction_text: Draupadi declares her vengeance satisfied and says Ashvatthaman, as a teacher's son, should be respected like a teacher. She asks Yudhishthira to wear the gem.

attributes.relationships: Ashvatthaman as teacher's son, Draupadi as mother of slain sons

extraction_text: Yudhishthira takes the gem and wears it on his head, honoring it as a teacher's relic.

attributes.significance: Symbol of victory and teacher's honor

extraction_text: Draupadi rises from her grief, and Yudhishthira consults Krishna again.

attributes.emotional_shift: Draupadi moves from sorrow to acceptance
